content: Obstructive lung disease refers to a group of pulmonary disorders characterized by structural abnormalities that lead to the collapse of the airways. Patients with obstructive lung disease typically experience shortness of breath, which arises from damage to the airways within the lungs. This damage impairs the ability to fully exhale air, resulting in an abnormally high volume of air remaining in the lungs even after maximal expiration. One of the primary causes of obstructive lung disease is prolonged exposure to substances that irritate and damage the lung epithelium and parenchyma. These irritants include cigarette smoke, air pollution, chemical fumes, and dust, among others. During the early stages of the disease, patients are often asymptomatic. However, as the disease progresses, symptoms become more pronounced. Common symptoms include a productive cough, difficulty breathing, wheezing, and a sensation of chest tightness. Diseases that fall under the category of obstructive lung disease include asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiolitis, bronchiectasis, heart failure, tuberculosis, cystic fibrosis, and lymphangioleiomyomatosis. These conditions are associated with an obstructive pattern on pulmonary function tests, which typically reveal an increase in total lung capacity (TLC) and residual volume (RV), along with a decrease in forced vital capacity (FVC), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), and the FEV1/FVC ratio. Pulmonary function tests, particularly spirometry, are essential in distinguishing obstructive lung diseases from restrictive lung diseases. Spirometry findings in obstructive lung diseases demonstrate the characteristic airflow limitation and help guide diagnosis and management.
